Tetratype now measures **what your hands are doing** and **what you get wrong**, not just how
long things take.

## Your hands

Every transition is classified against your keyboard layout: **same finger**, **scissor**,
**inward** or **outward roll**, **alternating**, **redirect**, **double tap**, **dead key**.
So `br` is no longer "slow" — it is a same-finger bigram, and the fix is different.

Expand any n-gram and each internal jump is labelled individually, so a slow tetragram
resolves into *which* movement is the problem.

Layouts: QWERTY (Spanish, default), QWERTY (US), Colemak, Dvorak. Dead keys are modelled
honestly — `á` is two presses, and the transition into it includes reaching for `´`.

## Your mistakes

Tetratype reads the character the test is waiting for *before* Monkeytype processes your
keystroke, so it knows what you owed and what you produced in the same instant — no lag.

- **Confusion table**: `r → t`, 15 times, same finger, 620 ms to recover.
- **Recovery cost.** A typo costs the fumble plus the backspace plus the retype — usually
  500–900 ms, normally more than the latency excess you were optimising. A correction only
  counts once you have actually rewound over the mistake; typing on past an error is counted
  separately as **left standing**.
- **Miss rate** per character and per transition, joined onto the n-gram table. An n-gram can
  now be slow, unreliable, or both — and you can tell which.

## When you break down

- **Speed against accuracy** — names the fastest interval band where you still hold accuracy.
  The answer to "how hard can I push?"
- **Within a session** — warm-up and fatigue, split after five idle minutes.
- **Day by day** — WPM and accuracy over the last 180 days.

Plus a per-n-gram **trend** (two exponentially weighted means, not a stored time series) and
a **context penalty**: how much more a pair costs inside longer n-grams than on its own.

## Export analysis

One button, one Markdown file: every table and curve, already labelled. Built to hand
straight to a language model — the README carries a prompt written against it that weighs
mistakes against slowness and reads your accuracy curve before telling you to go faster.

## Privacy

Still one permission (`storage`), still Monkeytype-only, still no network requests.

Naming a typo means reading one character of lookahead — the one you were about to type
anyway — stored only as part of an `expected → typed` pair. Single-character pairs cannot be
reassembled into text. **Track mistakes** in Settings turns it off entirely; error detection
then falls back to Monkeytype's own markup.

All the new data is bounded counters: 2 000 confusion pairs, 20 speed bands, 12 session
bands, 180 days. Nothing grows with how long you use it.

## Upgrading

Store schema is version 2. Version 1 profiles import unchanged — the new fields start empty
and fill in as you type.
